    if fx:
        t = t.flip(-1)
    if fy:
        t = t.flip(-2)
    if tr:
        t = t.transpose(-2, -1)
    return t

        super().__init__()
        self.Y = int(spec.Y)
        self.X = int(spec.X)
        self.n_place = int(spec.n_place)
        cells = self.Y * self.X
        self.K = (self.n_place + cells - 1) // cells
        self.padn = self.K * cells - self.n_place
        sq = self.Y == self.X
        lays = [l for l in LAYOUTS if sq or l[0] == 0]
        if len(lays) == 0:

        self.r1 = nn.Conv2d(WIDTH, WIDTH, 3, padding=1)
        self.r2 = nn.Conv2d(WIDTH, WIDTH, 3, padding=1)
        self.h3 = nn.Conv2d(WIDTH, HEAD, 3, padding=1)
        self.h1 = nn.Conv2d(WIDTH, HEAD, 1)

Between them, the candidates cover action layout set A, set B, obs fed under all 8 grid symmetries, and LayerNorm stems with gain-0.01 policy outputs, which helped with the input-scale issue seen in world 4. Any nonzero score tells us which set to split in round 2. If every candidate scores 0, round 2 should combine hedges and try type-minor layouts. One seed per trial means gaps under 0.1 are noise.
analyses.2: Plain set A scored 0.154 and plain set B scored 0. So, with the obs read as given, the true action layout is probably in A. Feeding the obs under all 8 symmetries raised set A to 0.393 and set B to 0.248. Extra views of the obs let the stem realign it, so they help even when the layout set misses the true frame. This is weak evidence that the obs is also reoriented, or that the extra views just make learning easier. The two LayerNorm and gain-0.01 variants did no better: 0 and 0.154. Inputs on the wrong scale are unlikely, so this round drops LayerNorm. Each result is one seed, so the 0.39 vs 0.25 gap is suggestive, not decisive. Round 2 splits set A into its 4 single layouts, each with the obs symmetries. Earlier worlds suggest the right one should score about 0.8 and the wrong ones 0. The two spare slots refine the set-A hedge, as a fallback if the split fails.
analyses.3: Set B without obs symmetries scored 0, while plain set A scored 0.15. So the action frame is probably in A relative to the obs as given. Adding the 8 obs symmetries made every layout learnable: each single layout scored 0.15-0.20 and none stood out. With every obs view available, the net can match any action layout, so that split could not identify the true layout. The 0.83 from r2c6 (ent_coef 0.01, 16 minibatches) suggests the recipe matters on this net, but it is one seed and results are bimodal. LayerNorm did not help (0 and 0.15), so mis-scaled inputs look unlikely. This round splits set A again without obs symmetries, on the better recipe. The correct layout should reach about 0.8-0.9 and the wrong ones 0. Two more trials test a single layout with symmetries and a higher entropy coefficient.
analyses.4: The split worked. With the new recipe (ent_coef 0.01, 16 minibatches), the single y-flip layout on the plain obs scored 0.955. Identity, transpose and x-flip each scored exactly 0, so this world's action rows are y-flipped, as in world 7. Plain set A scoring 0.15 fits this. The obs symmetries were not needed for alignment. Identity plus symmetries reached 0.89 only because the symmetry views include a y-flip. The recipe change mattered: the same set A + symmetries net went from 0.39 to 0.83 with no change to the net, although the two runs used different seeds. Raising ent_coef to 0.02 gave 0.80, no better. In this last round, every candidate is r3c3 with one refinement: lr 3e-3, 3 PPO epochs, global context in the head, 32 minibatches, gamma 0.95, or y-flip with the symmetries kept. Each targets a small gain or more robustness across seeds. With one seed, gaps under about 0.05 near 0.95 are noise.
